quotes.text: A pipeline isn't a tool you buy off a shelf. It's a habit with a machine attached, and the teams that get the most out of one usually changed how they work, rather than which software they installed.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Reframes CI/CD as a working habit rather than a product purchase.

quotes.text: If any test fails, the build is red and the team stops to fix it because almost green is still red.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: A memorable statement of the discipline continuous integration depends on.

quotes.text: Delivery means you can deploy at any time, and deployment means you actually do every time a change gets through.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Separates two commonly confused terms in a single sentence.

quotes.text: The version that passed in the test environment has to be the exact version that reaches production, or the test proved nothing.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: States the build-once-promote-the-artifact rule that protects every release.

quotes.text: A test like that teaches the whole team to ignore red, and once people ignore red, the pipeline is decoration.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Explains why flaky tests quietly destroy trust in automation.

chapters.title: The problem it was built to solve
Environments and the gate before production

takeaways: Continuous integration means merging small changes at least daily while an automated build and tests check every change.
Continuous delivery keeps software always releasable, while continuous deployment releases every passing change automatically.
Small changes, a single promoted artifact, trusted tests and a fast rollback path matter more than any specific pipeline tool.
hook: Manual releases and late merges make software changes slow and risky. This episode explains CI/CD pipelines in plain language for makers, admins and developers working with Azure DevOps, GitHub Actions or Power Platform. You learn what each stage checks, how delivery differs from deployment and which habits keep a pipeline trustworthy.
